title: One straight line across the crowd
allegory: A linear probe is like a referee allowed one straight chalk line across a crowded hall: if the line cleanly splits guests wearing 'true' badges from 'false' ones, the model keeps truth somewhere readable at that moment, and whether the model actually uses that line is a separate test where you shove guests across it and see if its verdict changes.
map: the hall at one moment of the evening
the residual stream at one layer of a frozen model
the activation vector for one statement
a linear probe: a weight vector w, score w·x + b
the arrow from the 'false' crowd's centre to the 'true' crowd's centre
shoving guests along the arrow to see if the verdict flips
patching the direction back in and measuring P(TRUE) − P(FALSE)

props.label: 'The city of Beijing is in China'

cap.1: Does a model 'know' that 'Beijing is in China' is true? You don't want to ask it. You want to read the answer off the numbers it holds inside.
cap.2: A linear probe: freeze the model, record activations at one layer and token, and train a tiny linear classifier on them. If it works, the property is linearly readable there.
cap.3: Probing tests whether a property is linearly decodable: fit w on frozen residual-stream activations at a chosen layer and position. It's the cheapest interp tool: one direction, one dot product, no retraining.

cap.1: Picture each sentence as a guest standing where its numbers put it. From above, true ones already crowd apart from false ones. One straight line splits them.
cap.2: Marks and Tegmark ran PCA on Llama-2-13B's layer-14 activations for true and false statements. With no labels at all, the top two components split them into two clouds.
cap.3: Unsupervised separation in the top principal components, before any probe is trained, is the first evidence that truth sits along a direction rather than smeared across the network.

cap.1: The simplest line: find the centre of each crowd and draw the arrow between them. To score a new sentence, see how far along that arrow it stands.
cap.2: MM (difference of means) is literally mean(true acts) − mean(false acts), and a sentence's score is w·x. LR (logistic regression) instead tilts w to fit the labels on the same activations.
cap.3: MM: w = μ₊ − μ₋, no optimisation. LR: w, b fit by logistic loss on sigmoid(w·x + b). Both give one direction in d_model; LR wins on accuracy and transfers near-ceiling across the three datasets.

chapters.name: Reading isn't using

right.title: MM probe
lines: bigger shift in the model's verdict

chapters.verdict: The line that reads best isn't always the line the model uses.

cap.1: Does the model use the line? Shove sentences along it inside the model and see if it changes its mind. The plain arrow moves it more than the accurate line.
cap.2: Add the scaled direction at layers 8 to 14 and measure P(TRUE) − P(FALSE) on a TRUE/FALSE prompt. LR wins on accuracy, but MM moves the verdict more: higher accuracy, weaker causal effect.
cap.3: MM gives the larger natural indirect effect when patched at the statement's final period and the first suffix token, despite LR's accuracy and transfer. Classification accuracy and causal relevance come apart.

chapters.name: Fooled by a shortcut
chapters.title: train on a row, test on a column

cap.1: Your probe scores 95% on true and false cities, so you call it a truth probe. Then it splits likely text from unlikely text, where nothing is true or false.
cap.2: True statements also tend to be the more probable text, so 'likely continuation' is a free confound. Check the off-diagonal transfer cells, and run `likely` as a negative control a truth probe should fail.
cap.3: A probe fits whatever separates the labels; models even linearly represent XORs of features, so 'truth XOR geography' can pass in-domain tests. Use transfer, direction cosines, a negative control, then patching.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Deception probes: trained on no lies, caught lies
Readable is not used: patch to check
Average only over the reply's tokens

cap.1: Apollo trained a probe on true facts told under 'be honest' and 'be deceptive' prompts, with no real lies, and it flagged deception before the lie was written.
cap.2: Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025): instructed pairs on Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct gave AUROC 0.96 to 0.999 on realistic deception scenarios. A cheap window onto what a model intends helps us understand and steer it.
cap.3: Their caveats: the probe drifts toward tracking morality, so honest confessions get flagged, and mean-pooling a partly deceptive reply can wash it out; average only over assistant tokens. Not yet a robust defence.

coda.title: Which way does your line lean? (toy: truth and likely-text as two directions)

params.label: lean toward 'likely text' (0 = pure truth, 1 = pure likelihood)

readouts.label: accuracy on the usual set (true goes with likely)
accuracy when truth and likelihood disagree
gap on the `likely` control (a truth probe: 0)

caption.1: Drag the lean. On the usual set accuracy stays perfect, since true and likely go together. Only the mismatched pairs and the control reveal which line you drew.
caption.2: Toy: each sentence has a truth coordinate and a likely-text coordinate, and the probe scores w·x with w = (1 − a)·truth + a·likely. Past a = 0.5 it calls 'false but likely' true, and any lean splits the control.
caption.3: When two features are collinear in training data, any w in their span fits in-domain. Decorrelated examples pin the direction down, and a negative control should read about 0. Bars show sigmoid(3·w·x).

where_else: Deception probes: the same tool aimed at intent instead of fact (Apollo Research, 2025)
OthelloGPT: probing a game-playing model for a board it was never shown
Steering vectors: the same kind of direction, added in to change behaviour rather than read out
Activation oracles: swapping the probe's one fixed yes/no question for open-ended ones

hamming.what: A tiny linear classifier trained on a frozen model's activations to test whether a property is linearly readable at that layer.
hamming.when: When you have one specific question about what a model represents (truth, deception, a board state) and labelled examples to ask it with.
hamming.why: It's the cheapest window into a model, one direction and a dot product, but it only shows what is readable; patching shows what the model uses.

object.title: The verdict ramp
object.subtitle: A table whose height is the probe's verdict 'true'; the cliff edge is the chalk line, across a slice of activation space.

cap.1: A table whose height is the probe's verdict 'true'. Across it runs a cliff: that's the chalk line. Here it splits by truth alone.
cap.2: Height = sigmoid(k·w·x), the probe's P(true) over a 2D slice of activation space: x is the truth direction, y the likely-text direction.
cap.3: A linear probe's output is constant along the hyperplane w·x = 0 and ramps across it; here w = (1 − a, a) in the (truth, likely) plane.

cap.1: From above: true sentences sit on the high side and false ones on the low side, whether or not they read as likely text. A real truth probe.
cap.2: With a = 0, 'true, unlikely' still scores high and 'false, likely' still scores low: the direction ignores likelihood.
cap.3: w = (1, 0) is orthogonal to the likelihood axis, so the `likely` control projects to the boundary: separation about zero.

cap.1: Lean the line toward likely text. The usual sentences still land on the right sides, but 'false, likely' now sits high and 'true, unlikely' sits low.
cap.2: In-domain points, where true and likely go together, score the same either way. Only points where the two disagree expose the lean.
cap.3: Collinear training features leave w underdetermined within their span; decorrelated examples are what pin it down.

cap.1: Fully leaning, this is a likelihood detector wearing a truth-probe label. It would split the `likely` control cleanly, which a truth probe shouldn't.
cap.2: This is the `likely` failure: the probe separates text with likely versus unlikely continuations, where nothing is true or false.
cap.3: Marks and Tegmark predict a genuine truth probe should not separate `likely`, which makes it a usable negative control.

cap.1: A steeper cliff along the same line is more confident, not more right. Where the cliff runs matters, not how sharp it is.
cap.2: Scaling w changes the probe's confidence but not its decision boundary: which side each sentence lands on stays the same.
cap.3: sigmoid(k·w·x) has the same zero set for every k > 0; calibration changes, but the ranking and AUROC do not.

cap.1: Reading is only half. Push sentences across the cliff inside the model and see if its own verdict flips: that's how you learn it uses the line.
cap.2: Patching the direction into layers 8 to 14 and measuring P(TRUE) − P(FALSE) tests use, not just readability.
cap.3: Causal validation: add ±α·w to residual activations; in Marks and Tegmark the MM direction gave the larger effect despite LR's higher accuracy.
